description: Compromise-boundary verification semantics (RFC-ACDP-0014 §7), completing the rot-001 scenario set. Given the verified rev-001 revocation for K1 (fingerprint sha256:139e3940…, compromised_since T = 2026-05-01T00:00:00.000Z) and a context whose body signature resolves to K1: a receipt-attested publish time strictly before T verifies as historically authorized (pre-compromise, receipt-attested); at-or-after T, or with no verifiable publish time, verification MUST fail closed under the strict profile. Scenarios E-G pin the fold's correctness across a superseding lineage (narrower successor, retraction, non-revocation successor); scenario H extends the same methodology to a widening successor published under the §10 interim `acdp:key-revocation` form, which §7's disregard clause MUST NOT mistake for a disarming non-revocation — an unconditional 0.3.0 obligation like A-G, since RFC-ACDP-0014 §10 already requires 0.3.0 consumers to treat the interim form as fully equivalent to the standard type.

revocation.note: The rev-001 golden key-revocation context, verified per RFC-ACDP-0014 §5 (producer-signed by K2; signer fingerprint != revoked fingerprint; visibility public).

body_under_test.note: The sig-001 golden context, signed by K1.

producer_did_document.note: The rot-001 DID document: K1 retained in verificationMethod only (NOT removed — RFC-ACDP-0014 §9: revocation does not require removal; the pre-T record needs the key material); K2 in verificationMethod and assertionMethod.

key-2.role: K2 — the current key, signer of the revocation

registry_receipt.note: The rcpt-001 golden receipt shape for the body under test. RFC-ACDP-0010 §8 verification is a precondition — an unverified receipt provides no publish time.
registry_receipt.note_on_efg: Scenarios E, F and G reuse one publish time chosen to sit STRICTLY BETWEEN the two boundaries in the lineage: T1 = 2026-05-01 <= 2026-05-20 < T2 = 2026-06-15. That placement is what makes a wrong fold observable rather than merely wrong internally — folding to the earliest T (correct) puts the body at or after the boundary and fails closed, while folding to the head's T (or to no T at all) puts it before the boundary and returns the same success verdict as scenario A. The two implementations disagree on the VERDICT, not just on an intermediate value.
registry_receipt.note_on_h: Scenario H's publish time sits STRICTLY BETWEEN lineage L3's two boundaries, the other way round from E/F/G: T4 = 2026-04-01 (Y, the interim-typed WIDENING correction) <= 2026-04-15 < T1 = 2026-05-01 (R1-triple-prime, the original). Folding correctly (earliest T across every revocation the lineage contains, interim-typed members included per RFC-ACDP-0014 §7) yields T4 and fails closed. A consumer that disregards Y — reading RFC-ACDP-0014 §7's 'not itself a revocation' test as a literal string match against `key-revocation` only, missing the §10 interim form `acdp:key-revocation` — falls back to R1-triple-prime's own T1 and returns success: the exact fail-open scenario G's clause exists to prevent, reached through the one successor type that clause's original wording did not explicitly name. This is an unconditional 0.3.0 obligation, not a 0.5.0 amendment: §10 already requires 0.3.0 consumers to treat the interim form as fully equivalent to the standard type, so a consumer that ignores Y was never conformant, even before this scenario existed to catch it.

revocation_lineage.note: Three SEPARATE revocation lineages, not one. RFC-ACDP-0003 §3.1 steps 5 and 6 make a lineage strictly linear — version must be previous.version + 1, and only the first body to supersede a given predecessor is accepted (the second gets superseded_target, HTTP 409) — so R2, X and Y could never all supersede R1 in a single lineage against a conformant registry. Scenarios E and F use lineage L1; scenario G uses lineage L2; scenario H uses lineage L3. All three are obtained by walking GET /lineages/{lineage_id} (RFC-ACDP-0004 §5.1), which returns every version ordered by version ascending with its own registry_state.

L1.note: A revocation superseded by a LATER-boundary revocation of the same signer class — the §4 supersedes row's permitted case.

members.label: R1
members.note: The rev-001 context. T1 — the EARLIEST boundary in the lineage, and therefore the effective one.

members.label: R2
members.note: A later, NARROWER boundary (T2 > T1). The publish is conformant — §4 permits a revocation to be superseded by another of the same signer class, and §3.1 step 3's agent_id equality is satisfied — but §4's earliest-T rule means it cannot shrink the effective window. A producer correcting a mistaken revocation this way annotates the record; it does not change any consumer's verdict.

retraction_for_scenario_F.note: Scenario F only. R1 is retracted per RFC-ACDP-0013 §6 after R2 supersedes it. The body stays retrievable and byte-identical (RFC-ACDP-0013 §8.1) and GET /lineages/{lineage_id} still includes it. Requires a registry advertising acdp-registry-lifecycle; a registry that does not advertise it cannot emit the retracted status at all (RFC-ACDP-0013 §6), so the scenario simply does not arise there.

L2.note: A revocation superseded by a context that is NOT a revocation. Distinct lineage_id from L1; R1-prime is an independent publication of the same revocation statement, so its own T is again T1.

members.label: R1-prime
members.note: T1 — the only boundary in this lineage, and still the effective one after X supersedes it.

members.label: X
members.note: A NON-revocation superseding a revocation, published under the same agent_id. RFC-ACDP-0003 §3.1 constrains supersession by existence, cross-registry, agent_id (step 3), lineage_id (step 4), version (step 5) and first-to-supersede (step 6) — but historically not by type, so every registry below acdp_version 0.5.0 accepts this publish; (0.5.0) a registry advertising acdp_version >= 0.5.0 now rejects it at the source (RFC-ACDP-0014 §4's predecessor-keyed rule, superseded_target/revocation_type_mismatch — see rev-003 O). Scenario G is the consumer-side defence (RFC-ACDP-0014 §7), which binds regardless of what any registry does or which acdp_version it advertises — a consumer MUST NOT rely on the §4 rejection existing.

L3.note: A revocation superseded by the §10 INTERIM-typed revocation form, widening (not narrowing) the boundary. Distinct lineage_id from L1/L2; R1-triple-prime is an independent publication of the same revocation statement, so its own T is again T1. This lineage can arise on any registry below acdp_version 0.5.0 (nothing there rejects an interim-typed publish, since the pre-0.5.0 supersedes-row check only fires for bodies literally typed key-revocation, and the >= 0.5.0 registry-side rejection rules introduced alongside this scenario do not exist on such a registry), or on a >= 0.5.0 registry serving a lineage whose interim-typed member was published before that registry upgraded (RFC-ACDP-0014 §10 explicitly preserves existing interim-form bodies' retrievability unchanged). The consumer-side obligation this scenario tests is unconditional at 0.3.0 regardless of which of these gave rise to the lineage.

members.label: R1-triple-prime
members.note: T1. A conformant successor per the §4 supersedes row IF the successor counts as 'a key-revocation' — which is exactly the question Y below poses.

members.label: Y
members.note: A WIDENING correction (T4 = 2026-04-01 is EARLIER than T1 — permitted, per the §4 supersedes row's 'widen, never narrow' rule) published under the §10 interim form, same agent_id. Not a disarming non-revocation like X in L2 above: Y is itself a revocation, just spelled the pre-0.3.0 way. RFC-ACDP-0014 §7's fold MUST count Y's T4, not disregard it — that is scenario H's point.

scenarios.name: A — receipt-attested publish time before T

expected.behavior: Receipt verifies per RFC-ACDP-0010 §8 with created_at = 2026-04-16T10:30:15.123Z < T. The context was published while K1 was still the producer's: verification proceeds under the RFC-ACDP-0010 §10 historical rule against K1 (verificationMethod-retained) and succeeds with the distinguishable status 'historically authorized (pre-compromise, receipt-attested)'. SDKs MUST NOT report it as fully current, and MUST NOT report it identically to the no-revocation rot-001 scenario A status — the revocation and its boundary MUST be visible in the verdict (suggested stage: key_revocation).

scenarios.name: B — receipt-attested publish time at or after T

expected.behavior: Identical retrieval except the (valid, verified) receipt carries created_at = 2026-05-03T09:00:00.000Z >= T. The signature is inside the compromise window and is not attributable to the producer. Verification MUST fail closed regardless of DID-document state and regardless of the receipt's validity — the receipt proves exactly when the registry accepted it, which is what places it after the boundary (RFC-ACDP-0014 §7 step 3).

scenarios.name: C — no receipt: publish time unverifiable

expected.behavior: The same body served without a registry_receipt (or with one failing RFC-ACDP-0010 §8). The bare body created_at MUST NOT be used as the boundary input (registry-assigned, unverifiable — RFC-ACDP-0008 §9.1); the context cannot be placed relative to T, and an unplaceable revoked-key signature is exactly the artifact an attacker mints freely. The strict profile (RFC-ACDP-0001 §5.11 / §9.2) MUST fail closed. Any pragmatic mode accepting other time evidence MUST be a non-default, explicitly-named opt-in, non-conformant with the strict profile (RFC-ACDP-0014 §7 step 4).

The same revocation statement arriving as a registry-attested context (agent_id = the registry's DID, metadata.revoked_key_controller = the producer DID — RFC-ACDP-0014 §6) MUST be classified 'registry-attested', distinguishable from 'producer-signed', and MUST NOT be silently collapsed into it: strict-profile default applies §7 for contexts served/receipted by that same registry and seeks corroboration before global application. A 'revocation' signed by K1 itself MUST be treated as unverified (§5 step 2) and triggers none of the §7 semantics.

scenarios.name: E — earliest compromised_since across a superseding lineage is effective

expected.behavior: Lineage L1, body_under_test receipt-attested at 2026-05-20T12:00:00.000Z. The effective boundary is T1 = 2026-05-01 (R1), NOT T2 = 2026-06-15 (R2, the head): RFC-ACDP-0014 §4's supersedes row and §7 both require the earliest compromised_since across a revocation lineage to be effective, so the fold is a MINIMUM over every member, not a lookup of the current one. 2026-05-20 >= T1, so verification MUST fail closed exactly as in scenario B. A consumer that folds to the head's boundary instead computes 2026-05-20 < T2 and returns scenario A's success verdict — accepting a signature the producer has disavowed, and doing so silently. That divergence in the VERDICT, not merely in an intermediate value, is what this scenario pins.

scenarios.name: F — a retracted revocation still counts in the fold

expected.behavior: Lineage L1 again, with R1 additionally retracted (RFC-ACDP-0013 §6) after being superseded. The effective boundary is STILL T1 and the verdict is STILL fail-closed. Retraction is a reliance signal on the record, not an un-revocation — RFC-ACDP-0014 §4 is explicit that there is no un-revoking a key, and RFC-ACDP-0013 §8.1 keeps the body retrievable and byte-identical — so a consumer MUST NOT drop R1 from its cache or exclude it from the fold because it was retracted. Note precisely what the retraction does and does not do here: R1 is already absent from /current because it is SUPERSEDED, so the retraction is not what hides it from a /current-based fold. The hazards the retraction does introduce are cache eviction on the retracted event and an explicit 'skip retracted members' filter over the lineage array — both of which narrow the window to T2 and flip this scenario to a false success. (Retracting the HEAD, R2, is the variant where /current itself breaks down: every member is then superseded or retracted and the endpoint returns 404 per RFC-ACDP-0013 §8.3, leaving a /current-based fold with no revocation at all.)

scenarios.name: G — a non-revocation supersession does not disarm the revocation

expected.behavior: Lineage L2: X (type 'analysis') supersedes R1-prime under the same agent_id. The revocation remains effective, the boundary remains T1, and the verdict is fail-closed. Per RFC-ACDP-0014 §7, a superseding context that is not itself a revocation of the same signer class (§2) MUST be disregarded for revocation-effectiveness. A consumer that folds by reading the head, or that treats 'superseded' as 'withdrawn', sees an innocuous analysis context, applies no boundary at all, and returns plain success — which is how an attacker holding the producer's current key neutralizes a safety broadcast without ever forging anything. This defence is deliberately consumer-side: it binds on upgrade alone and needs no registry cooperation, whereas any registry-side rejection reaches only the registries that adopt it. A consumer MUST NOT assume a registry filtered such a supersession out.

scenarios.name: H — an interim-typed widening successor still counts in the fold

expected.behavior: Lineage L3: Y (type 'acdp:key-revocation', the §10 interim form) supersedes R1-triple-prime under the same agent_id, WIDENING the boundary from T1 = 2026-05-01 to T4 = 2026-04-01. Unlike scenario G's X, Y IS a revocation — just spelled the pre-0.3.0 way — so RFC-ACDP-0014 §7's disregard clause does not apply to it: 'a revocation' for that clause's purposes means key-revocation OR the §10 interim form, matching §4's definition. The correct fold takes the earliest T across the whole lineage, T4, and the body_under_test's receipt-attested publish time (2026-04-15) falls at-or-after T4, so verification MUST fail closed. A consumer whose disregard test is a literal string match against `key-revocation` (missing the interim spelling) instead treats Y as if it were an unrelated non-revocation like G's X, falls back to R1-triple-prime's own T1 = 2026-05-01, finds 2026-04-15 < T1, and returns success — silently missing the fact that a legitimate WIDENING correction moved the true boundary earlier still. That is a fail-open on the exact class of correction §4's supersedes row exists to permit, reached precisely because the successor used the interim form scenario G's non-revocation case does not exercise.

notes: Alignment with rot-001: scenario A here refines rot-001 A (revocation present, boundary respected → pre-compromise variant of historically-authorized); rot-001 B (no receipt, no revocation → fail closed strict) and rot-001 C (K1 removed from verificationMethod → total kill, fail closed regardless of receipts or boundaries) are UNCHANGED by RFC-ACDP-0014. The earliest compromised_since across a superseding revocation lineage is effective (RFC-ACDP-0014 §4) — a supersession can widen but never quietly shrink the window. Scenarios E, F and G pin that end to end against a single publish time (2026-05-20, between T1 and T2), so each of the three ways a head-based fold goes wrong — reading the head's boundary, dropping a retracted member, or seeing a non-revocation at the head — produces an observably different VERDICT, not just a different internal number. Scenario H extends the same methodology to a fourth way a fold goes wrong — misreading a WIDENING successor published under the §10 interim form as a disarming non-revocation, per RFC-ACDP-0014 §7's clarified disregard clause — using a publish time (2026-04-15, between L3's T4 and T1) chosen the same way E/F/G's was, so the two readings of the disregard clause diverge on the VERDICT rather than an internal value. H is an unconditional 0.3.0 obligation like A-G, not a 0.5.0 amendment: §10 has required 0.3.0 consumers to treat the interim form as fully equivalent to the standard type since 0.3.0's own promotion, and §7's clause was only ever ambiguous about the specific disarm-test wording, not about whether the underlying obligation existed. No test_keypair: this fixture is behavioral end to end, and scripts/conformance-runner.py dispatches rev-* to arithmetic execution on that marker.
